big: One famous study says the mix of equity, debt and gold explains most of a portfolio's ups and downs. It is often quoted wrongly. Here is what it says, and what it does not.

lines: I spend weekends hunting for the best fund. My friend says that is wasted effort. Who is right?
Neither fully. A 1986 study by Brinson, Hood and Beebower looked at exactly this. Let us watch what changes the ride, and what changes it little.

alt: Three lines: an 80 percent equity portfolio with sharper and weaker picks, and a 40 percent equity portfolio
caps: Made-up decade. Equity swings from +33% to -20%. Debt gives 7% every year.
Two 80% equity portfolios: one has slightly sharper picks, one slightly weaker. Look how closely they move.
The third keeps the same sharper picks but holds only 40% equity. Its shape is very different.
Picks shifted the end value. The mix set the ride: deepest fall about 14% against 4%.

h: What the mix does to the worst year
alt: Two bars: worst year loss for an 80 percent equity portfolio and a 40 percent one
caps: Same decade, same picks. Only the equity share differs: 80% against 40%.
In the worst year the 80% portfolio loses about 14%. The 40% portfolio loses about 4%.
On ₹10 lakh that is about ₹1,42,000 lost against about ₹36,000.
Changing picks by a point moved the worst year by under 1 point. Changing the mix moved it by about 11.

title: Reading the finding fairly
stops: The mix shapes the ups and downs over time
Set the mix before choosing funds
90% of your rupee profit comes from the mix
Fund choice never matters at all
alt: A shield with true and false readings of the 1986 finding
caps: Brinson, Hood and Beebower (1986): asset allocation explained about 90% of the variation in returns over time.
That is about the shape of the ups and downs, not about 90% of your profit.
It means: set the mix first, then compare funds inside it.

q: A client says: the study proves 90% of my profit comes from the equity-debt-gold mix, so fund choice hardly counts. What is the accurate correction?
opts: Nothing needs correcting, because the study splits profit into asset mix and fund choice
The study is wrong, because stock selection explains most of the return in practice
The figure is true only for retirees, who hold a fixed mix and make no changes at all
The 90% says how much of the ups and downs the mix explains, not a share of profit
why: The study measured how return variation is explained. It never split a client's profit into two shares like this.
The finding says the opposite: the mix, not stock selection, explained most of the variation over time.
The study looked at portfolios generally. It was not limited to retirees or to fixed, unchanging mixes.
The finding is about variation of returns over time. It does not say that 90% of the rupees earned come from the mix.

q: Two portfolios hold the same funds with the same picks. One is 80% equity, the other 40%. In a year equity falls 22%, which statement fits?
opts: Both lose about the same, because the same funds give the same result in a falling year
The 40% portfolio loses more, because it holds less equity and so recovers less
The 80% portfolio loses far more, since the mix sets how much of the fall it takes
The 80% portfolio loses less, as its higher equity share shows stronger fund picking
why: The same funds in different weights fall by different amounts. The mix sets how much of the fall is taken.
Holding less equity means taking less of an equity fall. The 40% portfolio loses less, not more.
A bigger equity share takes more of the fall. With debt at 7%, 80% equity loses about 16% and 40% about 5%.
An equity share shows risk taken, not skill. A larger share simply takes a larger part of the fall.

q: A client with ₹30 lakh spends weeks choosing between two good flexi cap funds, but has not decided how much goes to equity at all. What is the right order?
opts: The mix first, since it shapes the ride, and fund choice inside it afterwards
Choose the best flexi cap fund first, then work out whatever mix that leaves him with
Pick the fund with the highest past return, as that settles the mix automatically too
Split the ₹30 lakh in equal parts across every fund that he has heard about so far
why: The mix controls how much risk the money takes. Picking between two good funds is the smaller decision.
Starting with the fund leaves the mix to chance. The bigger decision, how much equity at all, would go unmade.
A high past return does not set the mix. It says little about how much risk the whole portfolio carries.
Equal splitting across many funds is not a mix decision. It can leave the portfolio overweight in one asset.

q: Why can a multi-asset fund be described as outsourcing the biggest decision?
opts: It picks stocks for the client, which is where most of a portfolio's return comes from
A manager sets and keeps the equity, debt and gold weights that shape the ride
It guarantees a 90% share of the best asset in each year, whichever one that is
It removes the need to hold any equity, so the client no longer takes market risk at all
why: Stock picking is the smaller part by the research. The allocation is the decision that is being handed over.
The fund's process sets and rebalances the mix. That is the choice the research says drives the ups and downs.
No fund can promise a share of the best asset each year. That would need perfect foresight.
A multi-asset fund still holds equity and takes market risk. It only blends it with other assets.

pts: The mix of equity, debt and gold explains about 90% of the variation in a portfolio's returns over time (Brinson, Hood and Beebower, 1986).
That is about the ups and downs, not 90% of your profit. Picks matter at the margin; the mix sets the ride.
Decide the mix first, then pick funds inside it. A multi-asset fund hands the mix decision to a process.
